We want to understand what you meant by "the "Continue Shopping" part feels very prominent, almost maybe too much?", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The “Continue Shopping” area is positioned above “Place Order,” making it appear higher in the layout hierarchy than the checkout completion option.  
B) The “Continue Shopping” area spans nearly the full width of the lower section, which makes it visually dominate that button area.  
C) The “Place Order” area appears visually subdued compared with “Continue Shopping,” so the bottom section seems to emphasize returning to shopping over completing the order.  
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: C, I think. I mean, B is also true visually, and A maybe contributes, but the thing that stood out to me was that “Place Order” is greyed out and quiet while “Continue Shopping” is this strong black full-width button. So the page kind of feels like it’s asking me to leave checkout rather than finish it, unless the disabled state is intentional because the card fields are empty, which it probably is, but still... visually that’s where my eye goes first.

turns.q: What is it about the “Continue Shopping” area’s size and placement that makes it dominate the lower button section?
turns.a: It’s almost the full width of the content column, and it sits immediately after the payment box, so it feels like the next primary step, I think. The “Place Order” button is the same width, but because it’s below that and very pale grey, it reads more like a secondary or unavailable thing rather than the actual endpoint. Also the vertical spacing puts “Continue Shopping” in this kind of prominent break between the form and the final legal text, so my eye lands there first. I could be wrong, but if I were scanning quickly, I might assume that’s the main action and only notice “Place Order” after a second.

turns.q: How does the full-width treatment and proximity to the payment box make “Continue Shopping” read as more primary than “Place Order”?
turns.a: Because it comes right after the last input area, it sort of completes the form rhythm, if that makes sense — fields, fields, then big dark button. The “Place Order” button is also full-width, but it’s separated just enough and so low-contrast that it feels like an inactive backup option, or maybe a disabled state I’m meant to ignore until later. The dark fill on “Continue Shopping” is the strongest visual weight on the whole lower half, probably even more than the “Payment Details” heading. So, maybe unintentionally, the hierarchy says “after payment, click this,” even though semantically that button sends me away from the checkout, which is... a bit risky, I think.

turns.q: What design gap in the button styling or grouping makes “Continue Shopping” get the stronger filled treatment while “Place Order” appears separated and lower-contrast?
turns.a: I think the gap is that there isn’t a visible hierarchy rule tying the two actions together, like… they’re just stacked as two full-width bars, but the destructive—or not destructive, sorry, the exit action—gets the active black style. “Place Order” looks disabled, which may be valid because the payment fields are empty, but there’s no enabled-primary preview or explanation that says it becomes the main action after the form is complete. So the styling is mixing two different meanings, maybe: black equals primary action, grey equals unavailable, and that leaves “Continue Shopping” accidentally inheriting primary status. I’d expect “Continue Shopping” to be more like a text link or outlined secondary button near the top or under the order summary, maybe, while the checkout completion area stays reserved for the order action... unless there’s a reason I’m not seeing.
